name: Irish nationalism
summary: Irish nationalism holds that the Irish people own Ireland and have a sovereign right to govern it, free of rule by Britain, and that the nation is a continuous community with its own language, history and culture. Its thinkers give it an inclusive, non-sectarian idea of the nation, a democratic claim that the people are sovereign, and a claim that the nation controls its land and resources. The strands split over means (armed rising or constitutional and consent-based methods) and over the Crown and the economy; today unity is pursued by peaceful means with consent in both parts of the island.
scope: The mainstream tradition drawn from its own texts and thinkers: Tone and the United Irishmen, O'Connell's Repeal, Davis and Young Ireland (with Lalor and Mitchel as Pearse names them), Griffith's Sinn Féin policy, Hyde and the Gaelic revival, Pearse and the 1916 Proclamation, the First Dáil's Democratic Programme, Connolly's socialist strand, and the present consent-based aim in Article 3 and the 1998 Agreement. Positions held by only one strand (Pearse on war, Connolly on class, the 1950s republican programme on money) answer only where the sources show the others share them or oppose them. It leaves out dissident groups that reject the Agreement and the policies of Irish states and parties where they are not the movement's own doctrine (neutrality, Catholic social teaching, European Union membership).

keyFigures.name: Theobald Wolfe Tone
keyFigures.role: Founder of Irish republican separatism and the United Irishmen, whom Pearse calls the greatest of Irish political thinkers

keyFigures.name: Thomas Davis
keyFigures.role: Young Ireland thinker of an inclusive cultural nationality and the national language

keyFigures.name: Patrick Pearse
keyFigures.role: Leader of the 1916 Rising and a signatory of the Proclamation

sources.title: Proclamation of the Irish Republic (1916)
sources.author: Provisional Government of the Irish Republic (Clarke, Mac Diarmada, Pearse, Connolly, MacDonagh, Ceannt, Plunkett)
sources.usedFor: Sovereignty and the continuity of nationhood, equal rights and suffrage for men and women, religious and civil liberty, no sectarian division.

sources.title: Democratic Programme of the First Dáil (1919)
sources.author: First Dáil Éireann
sources.usedFor: Property subordinate to the public welfare, national control of resources, a right to a share of the produce of labour, care for children and the aged, trade on terms of mutual advantage.

sources.title: The Necessity for De-Anglicising the Irish Nation (1892)
sources.author: Douglas Hyde
sources.usedFor: Language revival, native culture, history and schooling, a cultural revival that is not partisan, the rejection of prosperity bought at the price of nationality.

sources.title: Collected Works of Padraic H. Pearse: Political Writings and Speeches (The Murder Machine, The Coming Revolution, Peace and the Gael, The Separatist Idea, The Spiritual Nation, The Sovereign People)
sources.author: Patrick Pearse
sources.usedFor: Sovereignty of nations and of the people, franchise, property under the public right, national resources, language and education, violence and arms, the sanctity and continuity of the nation.

sources.title: The Resurrection of Hungary: A Parallel for Ireland
sources.author: Arthur Griffith
sources.usedFor: The Sinn Féin policy: protection of Irish industry, rejection of free trade, the Act of Union as illegal, opposition to British government good or bad, the 1782 settlement.

sources.title: The Autobiography of Theobald Wolfe Tone, vol. 1 (ed. R. Barry O'Brien)
sources.author: Theobald Wolfe Tone
sources.usedFor: The United Irish aims: break the connexion with England, replace the denominations of Protestant, Catholic and Dissenter with the name of Irishman, equal representation of the people.

sources.title: Literary and Historical Essays
sources.author: Thomas Davis
sources.usedFor: An inclusive Irish nationality, the national language, national schooling, protecting duties under a native parliament, against sectarian ascendency.

sources.title: Select Speeches of Daniel O'Connell, M.P.
sources.author: Daniel O'Connell (ed. J. O'Connell)
sources.usedFor: The constitutional strand: Repeal of the Union with loyalty to the Crown, liberty of conscience.

sources.title: Labour in Irish History
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: The socialist strand: the nationalist cause tied to the common people and to common ownership; economic independence.

sources.title: Constitution of Ireland (1937, text of January 2020)
sources.author: The Irish people; Irish Statute Book
sources.usedFor: The national aims in Articles 1 to 3 and 8 (sovereignty, birthright, unity by peaceful means with consent, Irish as the first official language), the preamble, Article 6.

sources.title: The Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement, 1998
sources.author: Participants in the multi-party talks; British and Irish Governments (copy hosted by CAIN, Ulster University, via Wayback)
sources.usedFor: Consent principle and self-determination, power-sharing, peaceful means, decommissioning, the Irish language, the Irish Government's role in Northern Ireland.

sources.title: An Outline of the Main Political 'Solutions' to the Conflict
sources.author: Martin Melaugh, CAIN Web Service, Ulster University (drawing on McGarry and O'Leary)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly outline of the nationalist positions: a united Ireland by consent or by force, power-sharing with an Irish dimension, rejection of majority rule.

sources.title: Sinn Féin: Social and Economic Programme (1950s)
sources.author: Sinn Féin
sources.usedFor: The republican call to end British rule and Partition Government and unify Ireland (used for that aim only).

notes: Searched theme by theme in the full texts of the Proclamation, the Democratic Programme, Hyde, Pearse's political writings, Griffith's Resurrection of Hungary, Tone's autobiography, Davis's essays, O'Connell's select speeches, Connolly's Labour in Irish History, the Constitution (Articles 1 to 3, 8, 43), the Belfast Agreement and the CAIN outline. Government, world and globalism are thin because the tradition's texts are about national sovereignty, culture, the franchise and land rather than institutions or foreign policy. Not counted as the movement's own: neutrality, Catholic social teaching, EU membership, the 1950s republican programme's money policy (one party), and anything from unionist or British sources. Splits recorded as 0 (low): armed or peaceful means, the Crown, property, race and nation. Mainstream constitutional nationalists would not share Pearse's praise of war, so war-builds-character and armed-group-creates-revolution stay null; the O'Connell volume is mostly his 1810s speeches, so his later non-violence is not cited. Connolly's and Lalor's land and class positions are one strand, so land-redistribution and class-struggle-history stay null.
